summary: Linked lists are pointer gymnastics. Every problem reduces to one of five moves: traverse, reverse, insert, delete, or two-pointer chase. The dummy node and the three-pointer (prev/curr/next) dance solve 90% of the cases.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. Always reach for a dummy node
thoughtProcess.body: Any operation that may touch the head (insert at head, delete first, merge, partition) becomes uniform when you put a dummy before head. dummy.next is the always-correct return value.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. The three-pointer reversal dance
thoughtProcess.body: prev, curr, next. Save next, flip curr.next to prev, slide prev=curr, slide curr=next. This pattern is the atom of every reversal — full, partial (B..C), or in K-groups.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Two pointers solve 'from the end' in one pass
thoughtProcess.body: Stretch a fixed gap between fast and slow. When fast falls off, slow is exactly N from the end. No length computation needed.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. Visualize before coding
thoughtProcess.body: Draw 3-4 nodes on paper, label each arrow, then move them. The code is just the transcription. Skip this and you'll introduce a null-pointer bug every time.

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Edge cases live at head, tail, and 1-node lists
thoughtProcess.body: Always mentally test: empty list, single node, head operation, tail operation. If your code handles all four uniformly (usually thanks to dummy), it's correct.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Recursion ↔ iteration trade-off
thoughtProcess.body: Recursive LL is elegant but blows the stack on long chains (10^5+ nodes). Default to iterative for production; use recursion only when the structure (e.g., reverse-in-K-groups) genuinely simplifies.

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting to save next before flipping
commonMistakes.wrong:
curr.next = prev;
curr = curr.next;  // already null/prev
commonMistakes.why: Once you flip curr.next, you've lost the way forward. Always cache it first.

commonMistakes.title: Advancing pointer after a deletion
commonMistakes.wrong:
if (c.val == c.next.val) c.next = c.next.next;
c = c.next;  // skips a possible duplicate
commonMistakes.right:
if (c.val == c.next.val) c.next = c.next.next;
else c = c.next;
commonMistakes.why: After deleting, the new c.next could itself be a duplicate. Only advance when you did NOT delete.

commonMistakes.title: Off-by-one when walking to predecessor
commonMistakes.wrong: for (int i = 0; i < pos; i++) prev = prev.next;  // wrong if pos == 0 with no dummy
commonMistakes.why: Without a dummy, position 0 has no predecessor and the loop variant breaks. Dummy unifies all positions.

commonMistakes.title: Not null-checking fast before advancing
commonMistakes.wrong: for (int i = 0; i < B; i++) fast = fast.next;
commonMistakes.why: If B is larger than the list length, naive advance crashes with NPE.

commonMistakes.title: Returning the old head after reversal
commonMistakes.wrong:
// after full reversal
return head;  // head is now the TAIL
commonMistakes.right: return prev;  // prev is the new head
commonMistakes.why: After the loop, prev stands on the last node we flipped — that is now the head.

commonMistakes.title: Setting random pointer before next is rewired
commonMistakes.right: // Do interleave → set randoms → THEN unzip. Three separate passes.
commonMistakes.why: Each phase relies on the structure left by the previous one. Mixing them corrupts both.

commonMistakes.title: Recursive reverse leaves a cycle
commonMistakes.why: Without the null assignment, the old head still points forward — first two nodes form a cycle.

commonMistakes.title: Using == on Integer values from a list
commonMistakes.wrong: if (node.val == target)   // OK for int, fails silently for boxed Integer
commonMistakes.right:
// Use primitive int for ListNode.val.
// If you must compare Integer, use .equals().
commonMistakes.why: Java auto-unboxes only sometimes. == on Integer compares references, equal values may return false.

keyPatterns.name: Dummy + walk-to-predecessor
Three-pointer reversal
keyPatterns.when: Reverse the entire list, or a contiguous segment.

keyPatterns.name: Front-insertion partial reversal
keyPatterns.when: Reverse positions B..C in one pass.

keyPatterns.name: Two-pointer N-from-end
keyPatterns.when: Find or remove the Nth node counted from tail in one pass.

keyPatterns.name: Fast/slow (tortoise & hare)
keyPatterns.when: Cycle detection, find middle, find cycle entrance.

keyPatterns.name: HashMap clone
Interweave + unzip (O(1) clone)
examples: Copy List with Random Pointer (O(1) space)

keyPatterns.name: Group reversal
keyPatterns.when: Reverse every K-sized block, optionally leaving the leftover.
examples: Reverse Linked List in K Groups

edgeCases: Empty list (head == null) — return null immediately or let dummy handle it.
Single node — reversal returns same node; delete returns null; insert returns new head.
Operation at head — use a dummy so position 0 isn't special.
Operation at tail — make sure your loop reaches the last node (while c.next != null vs while c != null).
Position out of range — silently return unchanged, or return head.next if removing first.
K == 1 in K-group reversal — should return list unchanged.
B == C in partial reversal — no-op.
All duplicates — duplicate-removal should collapse to one node, not zero.
Long chain (10^5+) — recursive reversal will stack-overflow; prefer iterative.
Random pointer pointing to itself or null — interweaving copy must check c.random != null before dereferencing.
